questions.prompt: A PMOS has its source at \(V_{DD}\). Which condition puts it in saturation?
options: \(V_{GS} > V_{Tp}\) and \(V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_{Tp}\) with all quantities positive
\(V_{SG} < |V_{Tp}|\) and \(V_{SD}\) large
\(V_{SG} > |V_{Tp}|\) and \(V_{SD} \ge V_{SG} - |V_{Tp}|\)
questions.explanation: Write every PMOS voltage source-referenced and positive: \(V_{SG}\), \(V_{SD}\), \(|V_{Tp}|\). Then the NMOS rules carry over unchanged (the region test itself is the NMOS-regions prerequisite). Using \(V_{GS}\) and \(V_{DS}\) directly gives negative numbers and flipped inequalities (reader Sec. 9.5).

questions.prompt: A PMOS has \(V_S = 1.8\ \mathrm{V}\), \(V_G = 0.9\ \mathrm{V}\), \(|V_{Tp}| = 0.4\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mu_pC_{ox}W/L = 1\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\). Assuming saturation, find the drain current in µA.
questions.explanation: \(V_{SG} = 0.9\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(|V_{ov}| = 0.9 - 0.4 = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(I_D = \tfrac12(1\ \mathrm{mA/V^2})(0.5)^2 = 125\ \mu\mathrm{A}\), flowing out of the drain. Using \(V_G - V_{Tp} = 0.5\) by accident gives the same overdrive here only because \(V_S - V_G = V_G\); always form \(V_{SG}\).

questions.prompt: With the source fixed at \(V_{DD}\), you raise the PMOS gate voltage slightly. What happens to the drain current?
options: It decreases, because \(V_{SG}\) and the inversion charge fall
It increases, as it would for an NMOS
It is unchanged, since the source is fixed
It reverses direction
questions.explanation: Raising \(V_G\) lowers \(V_{SG}\), weakening the inversion layer. The small-signal model must agree: \(i_d = g_mv_{sg} < 0\). This wiggle test is the reader's sanity check for PMOS polarity.

questions.prompt: A PMOS common-source stage (source at \(V_{DD}\), drain load \(R_D = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) to ground) has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\) and \(r_o = 50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find the small-signal voltage gain \(v_{out}/v_{in}\).
questions.explanation: The supply is an AC ground, so the model is identical to the NMOS stage: \(A_v = -g_m(r_o\parallel R_D) = -2\ \mathrm{mS}\times8.33\ \mathrm{k\Omega} \approx -16.7\). It is still inverting; a positive answer comes from flipping the sign once for the PMOS and again for the stage.

questions.prompt: Which small-signal model is correct for a saturated PMOS?
options: \(g_mv_{gs}\) from source to drain
The same as the NMOS: \(g_mv_{gs}\) from drain to source, i.e. \(g_mv_{sg}\) from source to drain, with \(r_o\) between drain and source
\(-g_m\) in place of \(g_m\) in the NMOS model, with the source at the bottom
Just \(r_o\); the PMOS has no controlled source
questions.explanation: Drawn upside down, the PMOS model is the NMOS model: \(g_mv_{gs}\) drain-to-source equals \(g_mv_{sg}\) source-to-drain. A negative \(g_m\) would double-count the flip; \(g_m\) is always positive.

questions.prompt: A PMOS with \(\mu_pC_{ox} = 100\ \mu\mathrm{A/V^2}\), \(W/L = 20\) and \(|V_{Tp}| = 0.45\ \mathrm{V}\) has its source at 1.8 V. What gate voltage (V) gives \(I_D = 200\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) in saturation?
questions.explanation: \(|V_{ov}| = \sqrt{2(200\ \mu\mathrm{A})/(2\ \mathrm{mA/V^2})} = 0.447\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(V_{SG} = 0.897\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(V_G = 1.8 - 0.897 = 0.903\ \mathrm{V}\). Answering 0.897 V gives \(V_{SG}\), not the gate voltage.

questions.prompt: In the PMOS common-source stage, is the small-signal gain inverting?
options: No: a PMOS flips the sign, so the stage is non-inverting
Only if \(R_D > r_o\)
Yes: raising \(v_{in}\) lowers \(v_{sg}\) and the current into \(R_D\), so \(v_{out}\) falls
It depends on whether the supply is positive
questions.explanation: Use the wiggle test: up at the gate means less current pushed into the load, so the output goes down. Both device types give \(-g_m(r_o\parallel R_D)\).

questions.prompt: A PMOS has its source at 2.5 V, \(V_G = 1.5\ \mathrm{V}\), \(|V_{Tp}| = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mu_pC_{ox}W/L = 2\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\); its drain drives \(R_D\) to ground. What is the largest \(R_D\) (kΩ) that keeps it saturated?
questions.explanation: \(I_D = \tfrac12(2)(0.5)^2 = 0.25\ \mathrm{mA}\). Saturation needs \(V_{SD} \ge V_{SG} - |V_{Tp}| = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\), i.e. \(V_D \le 2.0\ \mathrm{V}\) (equivalently \(V_D \le V_G + |V_{Tp}|\)). So \(R_D \le 2.0/0.25 = 8\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Using \(V_D \ge V_G - |V_{Tp}|\), the NMOS form, flips the limit.

questions.prompt: A saturated PMOS has gate and source fixed. Its drain voltage rises by a small \(v\). What happens to the current flowing out of the drain?
options: It rises by \(v/r_o\)
It is unchanged; \(r_o\) does not apply to PMOS
It falls by \(g_mv\)
It falls by \(v/r_o\), since \(V_{SD}\) shrinks
questions.explanation: A higher drain means less \(V_{SD}\); channel-length modulation then lowers the current by \(v/r_o\). The \(g_m\) term needs a gate-source change.

questions.prompt: Preview of high-impedance loads: an NMOS CS stage uses a PMOS with its source at \(V_{DD}\) and gate at a fixed bias as its load. What does that PMOS look like to the signal?
options: A resistance \(r_{op}\) from the output to AC ground
A short to \(V_{DD}\)
A resistance \(1/g_{mp}\)
An open circuit with no effect on gain
questions.explanation: Gate and source are both AC grounds, so \(v_{sg} = 0\) and only \(r_o\) remains. That is the point of a current-source load: a large resistance without a large DC drop.

questions.explanation: The PMOS contributes only \(r_{op}\), in parallel with \(r_{on}\): \(A_v = -g_m(r_{on}\parallel r_{op}) = -1\ \mathrm{mS}\times50\ \mathrm{k\Omega} = -50\).

questions.prompt: Preview of mirror loads: why is a diode-connected PMOS always saturated?
options: Because PMOS devices cannot enter triode
\(V_{SD} = V_{SG}\), which always exceeds \(V_{SG} - |V_{Tp}|\)
Because its source is at \(V_{DD}\)
Because its current is fixed
questions.explanation: Tying gate to drain forces \(V_{SD} = V_{SG}\). The saturation condition then holds whenever the device conducts.
